z-m-07-01.title: Is the product of a two-digit number and a one-digit number always a three-digit number?
z-m-07-01.topic: Deciding how many digits the product of (two-digit number)×(one-digit number) has
z-m-07-01.goal: Know that a few correct multiplication examples don't make 'always,' make your own examples where the product of a two-digit number and a one-digit number is a two-digit number, and say when it becomes a three-digit number.
z-m-07-01.material:
Doyun solved multiplication problems and said this.
'37×4=148, 52×6=312, 78×9=702. The product of a two-digit number and a one-digit number is always a three-digit number!'
(Here the two-digit number is a number from 10 to 99, and the one-digit number is a number from 2 to 9. 37×4 is read as 'thirty-seven times four.')
z-m-07-01.thinking.0: Examine whether many correct examples guarantee 'always'
z-m-07-01.thinking.2: State the criterion that separates when it holds from when it doesn't
z-m-07-01.prereq.0: Read multiplication expressions of a two-digit number and a one-digit number and find the value (Grade 3 level)
z-m-07-01.prereq.1: Know that 100 is the first three-digit number
z-m-07-01.s.s1.prompt: What do you think of what Doyun said? Judge within the fixed ranges: two-digit numbers are 10 to 99 and one-digit numbers are 2 to 9.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write side by side the numbers Doyun tested, 37, 52, and 78, and the numbers he multiplied by, 4, 6, and 9, and find what cases he did not test.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.hint.1: Multiply the two smallest numbers in the range and the two largest numbers, and estimate about what range the product is in.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.o.a: All three examples are right, so Doyun's statement is right
z-m-07-01.s.s1.r.a: Examples being right and being right 'always' are different. You need to look at whether there are cases left that haven't been tested.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.o.b: It can be a three-digit number or a two-digit number
z-m-07-01.s.s1.r.b: This is the idea that the number of digits of the product can change depending on the sizes of the two numbers multiplied. It gets clearer if you make examples yourself and check.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.o.c: You multiplied by a one-digit number, so the product is always a two-digit number
z-m-07-01.s.s1.r.c: Just because a two-digit number is multiplied by a one-digit number doesn't make the product a two-digit number too. Look at how many digits the product of 78×9 that Doyun gave has.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.o.d: There are also cases where the product is a four-digit number
z-m-07-01.s.s1.r.d: Multiplying the two largest numbers gives the largest product. If you estimate about how much 99×9 is, you can tell whether it goes up to four digits.
z-m-07-01.s.s1.explain: The smallest product in the range is 10×2=20 and the largest product is 99×9=891. So the product can be a two-digit number or a three-digit number, and it cannot be a four-digit number.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.prompt: Make two examples with different products that show Doyun's statement is wrong. Choose a two-digit number a (10 to 99) and a one-digit number b (2 to 9) so that the product is not a three-digit number.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.hint.0: Pick small numbers first and multiply, and check how many digits the product has.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.hint.1: Choose one a, then change b to 2, 3, 4, ... and find where the product first becomes a three-digit number.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Make a a natural number from 10 to 99.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.ok.c2: b is a one-digit number (2 to 9).
z-m-07-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Make b a natural number from 2 to 9.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.ok.c3: The product is less than 100, so it is not a three-digit number. Doyun's statement is broken.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The product is a three-digit number or more. Change a or b so that the product gets smaller.
z-m-07-01.s.s2.explain: For example, 12×3=36, 20×4=80, and 45×2=90 are all two-digit numbers. 50×2=100 is the start of three-digit numbers, so it is not an example. Even one counterexample breaks 'always.'
z-m-07-01.s.s3.prompt: What would you like to tell Doyun? Using the examples you just made, write why he is wrong, and also write when the product becomes a three-digit number.
z-m-07-01.s.s3.hint.0: You may use the multiplication expressions from the examples you made first as they are.
z-m-07-01.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what number is the boundary between two-digit and three-digit numbers.
z-m-07-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In your example, did you calculate again to check that the product of the two-digit number and one-digit number really is a two-digit number?
z-m-07-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write knowing that one example is enough to break 'always'?
z-m-07-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you state when it becomes a three-digit number with numbers (for example, 99×9) or a criterion (100 or more)?
z-m-07-01.s.s3.model.0: What Doyun said isn't always right. There are cases where it is a two-digit number, like 12×3=36. If the two numbers are large and the product goes over 100, it becomes a three-digit number.
z-m-07-01.s.s3.model.1: No. 20×4=80 is a two-digit number. The larger the two numbers multiplied, the larger the product, so it can become a three-digit number like 99×9=891.
z-m-07-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that says 'the larger the numbers' instead of the criterion '100 or more' is also fine.

z-m-07-02.title: Can we find the larger number by comparing only the digits after the decimal point?
z-m-07-02.topic: Comparing the sizes of one-decimal-place numbers (the number before and after the decimal point)
z-m-07-02.goal: Know that decimals must be compared starting from the number before the decimal point, and tell apart the cases where the method of comparing only the digits after the decimal point works from those where it doesn't.
z-m-07-02.material: We measured the lengths of three ribbons and they were 0.9 m, 1.2 m, and 0.4 m. Hyeonu wanted to place them in order from the shortest ribbon and thought as follows. (0.9 is read 'zero point nine' and 1.2 is read 'one point two.')
z-m-07-02.thinking.0: Find the line in a solution that skipped ahead without evidence
z-m-07-02.thinking.1: Make several numbers within a given range
z-m-07-02.thinking.2: Sort out the conditions under which a method works
z-m-07-02.prereq.0: Meaning, reading, and writing of one-decimal-place numbers (0.1, 1/10), and reading a number line (Grade 3 level)
z-m-07-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in Hyeonu's thinking that has a wrong part.
z-m-07-02.s.s1.hint.0: First work out which of 0.9 m and 1.2 m is longer than 1 m.
z-m-07-02.s.s1.hint.1: Mark 0, 1, 2 on a number line and place 0.4, 0.9, 1.2 on the marks.
z-m-07-02.s.s1.line.0: The ribbon lengths are 0.9 m, 1.2 m, and 0.4 m.
z-m-07-02.s.s1.line.1: We just compare the digits after the decimal point. They are 9, 2, and 4.
z-m-07-02.s.s1.line.2: Placing from smallest, 2, 4, 9, so the order is 1.2 m, 0.4 m, 0.9 m.
z-m-07-02.s.s1.line.3: So 1.2 m is the shortest and 0.9 m is the longest.
z-m-07-02.s.s1.explain: The starting point is that line 2 compared only the digits after the decimal point. Decimals must be compared starting from the number before the decimal point (1 and 0). 1.2 is greater than 1 and 0.9 is less than 1, so 1.2 is larger. Line 3 just followed the method in line 2, and in line 4 that mistake showed up in the conclusion '1.2 m is the shortest.' The right order is 0.4 m, 0.9 m, 1.2 m.
z-m-07-02.s.s2.prompt: Write three different one-decimal-place numbers (numbers in units of 0.1) greater than 0.9 and less than 1.5.
z-m-07-02.s.s2.hint.0: Continue the numbers one at a time, growing by 0.1 from 0.9.
z-m-07-02.s.s2.hint.1: Stop before reaching 1.5, and check that all the numbers you wrote are in units of 0.1.
z-m-07-02.s.s2.ok.c1: It is greater than 0.9 and less than 1.5.
z-m-07-02.s.s2.fail.c1: It must be greater than 0.9 and less than 1.5. Look at the numbers between the two on the number line.
z-m-07-02.s.s2.ok.c2: It is a one-decimal-place number (in units of 0.1).
z-m-07-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Write it as a number in units of 0.1 (one-decimal-place number). Example: 0.4, 1.2
z-m-07-02.s.s2.explain: The one-decimal-place numbers between 0.9 and 1.5 are 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, and 1.4, five of them. Going 0.1 more from 0.9 is 1.0, and it must fall short of 1.5.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.prompt: When does Hyeonu's method of 'comparing only the digits after the decimal point' work?
z-m-07-02.s.s3.hint.0: Make a few pairs where the number before the decimal point is the same, like 0.4 and 0.9, and 1.2 and 1.7, and compare them with the two methods.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.hint.1: Also make a few pairs where the number before the decimal point is different, and check whether the result of comparing with the same method matches the real one.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.o.a: It always works when there is one digit after the decimal point
z-m-07-02.s.s3.r.a: 1.2 and 0.9 also have one digit after the decimal point, but the method was wrong. The number of digits after the decimal point alone doesn't separate the cases.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.o.b: It works only when the number before the decimal point is 0
z-m-07-02.s.s3.r.b: It is true that it works when the number before is 0, like 0.4 and 0.9. But check whether it also works when the number before is the same 1, like 1.2 and 1.7.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.o.c: It works when the numbers before the decimal point are equal
z-m-07-02.s.s3.r.c: If the numbers before are equal, you only need to compare the remaining part. If the numbers before are different, you must compare starting from the numbers before.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.o.d: It works when the digits after the decimal point are different
z-m-07-02.s.s3.r.d: 1.2 and 0.9 have different digits after the decimal point, but it was wrong. The digits being different is not enough.
z-m-07-02.s.s3.explain: When the numbers before the decimal point are equal, comparing only after the decimal point is fine. For example, for 1.2 and 1.7, comparing 2 and 7 shows 1.7 is larger. If the numbers before are different, you must compare starting from the numbers before.

z-m-07-03.title: I divided the number on a card by 6 and the quotient was 7. What is the number on the card?
z-m-07-03.topic: Finding the range of the dividend from the quotient and remainder of a division with a remainder
z-m-07-03.goal: Know that the quotient alone doesn't fix the dividend to one number, point out the missing information (the remainder), and find several numbers that fit the conditions and the largest number.
z-m-07-03.material: Soyul covered a number card with her hand and said, 'The number on this card is a natural number. I divided it by 6 and the quotient was 7.' Soyul hasn't yet said whether there is a remainder or not.
z-m-07-03.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is enough
z-m-07-03.thinking.1: Make several numbers that fit the conditions
z-m-07-03.thinking.2: Explain the range the remainder can be
z-m-07-03.prereq.0: Know the meaning of quotient and remainder in a division with a remainder (Grade 3 level)
z-m-07-03.s.s1.prompt: Can the number on the card be fixed to one from Soyul's words alone? What more would you need to know to fix it to one?
z-m-07-03.s.s1.hint.0: First write the smallest number whose quotient is 7. Add 1, 2, 3, ... to it and check whether the quotient is still 7.
z-m-07-03.s.s1.hint.1: Write out all the candidates, and find what one more piece of information would leave only one.
z-m-07-03.s.s1.o.a: You need to know more about how big the remainder is
z-m-07-03.s.s1.r.a: Even if the quotient is the same, if the remainder differs, the dividend differs. If you know the remainder, you can fix it to one of the candidates.
z-m-07-03.s.s1.o.b: You need to know more about whether it is odd or even
z-m-07-03.s.s1.r.b: If you know odd or even, the candidates decrease, but they aren't fixed to one. Count how many even candidates and how many odd candidates you can make.
z-m-07-03.s.s1.o.c: You need to know more about whether the divisor 6 is right
z-m-07-03.s.s1.r.c: Soyul has already told us the divisor 6. What isn't fixed yet is another part.
z-m-07-03.s.s1.r.d: 42 is one of the candidates, but if there is a remainder, it is not 42. Soyul didn't say it divides evenly.
z-m-07-03.s.s1.explain: When the quotient is 7, the number on the card is one of 42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47 (the remainder is 0 to 5). If you know the remainder, it is fixed to one. With odd or even alone, 3 are left each.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.prompt: Say the number on the card is not divisible by 6. Write three different numbers on the card whose quotient is 7 and which have a remainder.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether there is a remainder after taking 6 away from the number on the card 7 times.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.hint.1: Divide each number between 42 and 48 by 6 one at a time and check whether the quotient is 7 and the remainder is not 0.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The number on the card is a natural number.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Make the number on the card a natural number of 1 or more.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The quotient when divided by 6 is 7.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The quotient when divided by 6 is not 7. Count how many times 6 can be taken away.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.fail.c3: It divides evenly by 6. Change it to a number whose remainder is not 0.
z-m-07-03.s.s2.explain: The numbers whose quotient is 7 and which have a remainder are 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, five of them. They are 42 plus the remainders 1 to 5.
z-m-07-03.s.s3.prompt: What is the largest number the number on the card could be? Explain why that number is the largest by connecting it to the remainder.
z-m-07-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write the numbers the remainder could be one at a time from 0 and look at where you must stop.
z-m-07-03.s.s3.hint.1: Compare it with the smallest number whose quotient is 8.
z-m-07-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that dividing the number you wrote by 6 really gives a quotient of 7?
z-m-07-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say why the remainder can't be 6 or more?
z-m-07-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write the connection that when the remainder is the largest, the dividend is also the largest?
z-m-07-03.s.s3.model.0: It is 47. The remainder must be less than the divisor 6, so the largest remainder is 5. 42 plus 5 is 47.
z-m-07-03.s.s3.model.1: It is 47. When divided by 6 the remainder can only be 0 to 5, so when the remainder is 5, 42+5=47 is the largest.
z-m-07-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is an explanation that starts from 6×7=42 and adds the remainder.

z-m-07-04.title: What color is the 25th bead of the bead necklace?
z-m-07-04.topic: Matching position (number) and color in a repeating arrangement
z-m-07-04.goal: Know what assumption you make when guessing a far-off value from a rule seen only in part, tell how judgment and confidence change with new information, and find the rule for numbers where the same color comes up.
z-m-07-04.material: Yoona is making a necklace, counting the beads from the front as 1st, 2nd, 3rd, ... The bead colors are three: red, blue, and yellow, and there seems to be a rule for the colors she threads. I will tell you the colors only in words.
z-m-07-04.thinking.0: Guess a rule from part of the data and test it
z-m-07-04.thinking.1: Revise judgment and confidence with new information
z-m-07-04.thinking.2: Find the wrong line in a solution
z-m-07-04.thinking.3: Make numbers that fit the rule yourself
z-m-07-04.prereq.0: Counting things in a line by numbering them 1st, 2nd, ...
z-m-07-04.prereq.1: Reading arrangements where colors or shapes repeat (Grade 3 level)
z-m-07-04.s.s1.prompt: Let's guess as we learn the bead colors little by little. At each step, choose what you think is most fitting.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.hint.0: Write the beads known so far side by side, pairing numbers and colors.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.hint.1: Find the number where the same color arrangement starts again for the first time.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.info: The colors of beads 1 to 6, in order, are red, blue, blue, yellow, red, blue.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: What color do you think the 7th bead will be?
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.after: If you take red, blue, blue, yellow to repeat, the 7th is blue. But we have seen only 6, so there is still the chance of another rule. So both 'it seems to be blue' and 'it is too early to decide' are reasonable at this step.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is a guess that red, blue, blue, yellow repeat. We have only gone a bit past one set, so the confidence is not large.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Did you think that since yellow came at the 4th, it will come at the 7th too? Look at the gap between the number where yellow came and number 7.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You think that since red came at the 5th, red will continue. Look at what color the 6th, right after the 5th, was.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: We can't decide yet from just 6
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Being careful because few beads are visible is a good attitude. Still, look at whether there is a clue you can find in the visible beads.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Next, the colors of beads 7 to 12, in order, were blue, yellow, red, blue, blue, yellow. Now beads 1 to 12 are all confirmed.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Supposing the rule continues, what color do you think the 25th bead will be?
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.after: Up to 12, the same set of 4 repeated three times. Then the 24th is the last of the sixth set (yellow), and the 25th is the first bead of a new set, red. But 'the rule continues' is an assumption, so 'we can't decide yet' is also reasonable caution.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: List the numbers where yellow came, 4, 8, 12, and continue writing to see whether 25 is among them.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: We've only seen 12, so we can't decide yet
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Being careful is good, but if you count how many times the same pattern repeated within 12, you can find more clues.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Continue writing the numbers where blue came, 2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 11, and check whether 25 is among them.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is a judgment that took the sets to repeat every 4 and pointed out where 25 falls in a new set.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.info: It's new news. After the necklace was finished, we looked at the 30th bead and it was yellow. (We still don't know beads 13 to 29.)
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: What happens to your thinking about the 25th bead now?
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.after: If the rule held, the 30th would be blue (30 is the 2nd place after passing 7 sets of 4). But it was yellow, so the rule may have changed somewhere between 13 and 30. If the change was after 25, the 25th stays red, and if before, it could change. So 'red, but less certain' and 'can't decide' are reasonable, and 'certain' or 'yellow' lack a basis.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The 30th is yellow, so the 25th is yellow too
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The 30th and 25th are different numbers. Think about whether the 30th being yellow directly fixes the color of the 25th.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Regardless of the 30th, the 25th is certainly red
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: First check whether the 30th is the color the rule gives. Work out what color the 30th should be if the rule held.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: I still think it's red but I'm less confident than at first
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a judgment that even if the new information can shake the rule, if the shaken place is after 25, the 25th may stay the same.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The rule may have changed partway, so the 25th can't be decided
z-m-07-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Since we don't know where the rule changed, this is a careful judgment. It depends on whether the changed place is before or after 25.
z-m-07-04.s.s1.reflect: If you decided the 25th is red, did the news about the 30th change the judgment itself, or only lower your confidence? Explain why how much you trust a rule seen only in part depends on how far you have checked.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.prompt: Seoyun assumed the rule continues to the 25th and found the color of the 25th bead like this. Choose the line that has a wrong part.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.hint.0: Try Seoyun's method on the 6th or 7th bead whose color you already know, and compare with the real color.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.hint.1: Write side by side the colors of beads numbered 1, 5, 9, 13 and look at what Seoyun's method missed.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.line.0: The beads repeat red, blue, blue, yellow. One set is 4 beads.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.line.1: 25 divided by 4 gives quotient 6 and remainder 1.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.line.2: The quotient is 6, so the 25th bead is the same color as the 6th bead.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.line.3: The 6th bead is blue, so the 25th bead is blue too.
z-m-07-04.s.s2.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The quotient only tells which set it is, and the remainder tells the position within the set. If the remainder is 1, it is the same color as the 1st bead of the set (red). If you use the same method on the 6th bead whose color you know, the quotient of 6 divided by 4 is 1, so it matches the 1st bead (red), but the real 6th is blue. The 'blue' in line 4 is a result that came from the mistake in line 3. Found correctly, the 25th is red.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.prompt: Supposing the red, blue, blue, yellow rule continues, find and write three different numbers of beads that are yellow. (Numbers from 1 to 40)
z-m-07-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write the colors of beads 1 to 12 with their numbers and mark all the numbers that have yellow.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.hint.1: Look at the gaps between the marked numbers and continue with the same gap up to 40.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.ok.c1: It is a number between 1 and 40.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.fail.c1: Make the number a natural number from 1 to 40.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.ok.c2: It is a number where yellow comes.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.fail.c2: The bead at this number is not yellow. Starting from the number where yellow first appears, count how many numbers apart yellow comes.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.explain: Yellow is the last bead of a set (4 beads), so it is at numbers counted by 4s, like 4, 8, 12, .... From 1 to 40 there are ten: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.prompt: Write what the numbers you found have in common, and say why yellow comes at those numbers.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.hint.0: Write the numbers you found in order from smallest and write the differences between them.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.hint.1: Recall what place within a set yellow is.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the numbers you wrote with the table to check they are all yellow?
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you state what they have in common as the gap between the numbers or the way of dividing?
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Did you include in the explanation what place within a set yellow is?
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.model.0: 4, 8, and 28 are all multiples of 4. A set is 4 beads and yellow is the last of the set, so yellow comes every 4 beads.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.model.1: When the number is divided by 4, the remainder is 0. Yellow is the fourth bead of a set, so it is only at numbers whose remainder is 0.
z-m-07-04.s.s3.because.modelNote.1: This is an answer that puts it as 'numbers that divide evenly.'

z-m-07-05.title: If we change the numbers in the top row, does the pattern of the addition table change too?
z-m-07-05.topic: The pattern of how numbers change when moving across, down, or diagonally in an addition table
z-m-07-05.goal: Know that when moving between boxes in an addition table, how much the number changes is set by how much the header numbers of the rows and columns change, and use this to design a table with the pattern you want on your own.
z-m-07-05.material:
We made an addition table. The numbers in the left column are 1, 2, 3, 4 and the numbers in the top row are 2, 4, 6, 8. In the box where a row and column meet, write the sum of the two numbers.

  + |  2   4   6   8
----+----------------
  1 |  3   5   7   9
  2 |  4   6   8  10
  3 |  5   7   9  11
  4 |  6   8  10  12

(Read in words: the first row is 3, 5, 7, 9 / the second row is 4, 6, 8, 10 / the third row is 5, 7, 9, 11 / the fourth row is 6, 8, 10, 12.) In the textbook's addition table the top row is 1, 2, 3, 4, so each step one box to the right makes the number 1 bigger.
z-m-07-05.thinking.0: Predict the pattern of the table and check it
z-m-07-05.thinking.1: Find wrong reasoning in moves in several directions

z-m-07-05.s.s1.r.d: Look at how much the top row changes from 2 to 4 and from 4 to 6. That change shows up in the sum as it is.

z-m-07-06.title: If you stick two identical right triangles together, do you always get a rectangle?
z-m-07-06.topic: Shapes made by sticking two identical right triangles together (shape and perimeter)
z-m-07-06.goal: Test the claim 'always' by changing the sides and ways of sticking to find a counterexample, and explain how the perimeter changes as the stuck side is hidden.
z-m-07-06.material:
There are two sheets of colored paper shaped like right triangles. The two have exactly the same size and shape. The two sides next to the right angle are 3 cm and 4 cm long, and the longest side is 5 cm. Stick the two together along sides of equal length, exactly, with no gap or overlap, to make a new shape. You may flip or turn the paper before sticking it.
Seoa said, 'If you stick two identical right triangles together, it's always a rectangle!'
(3 cm is read 'three centimeters.')
z-m-07-06.thinking.0: Tell apart when the claim holds and when it doesn't
z-m-07-06.thinking.1: Find counterexamples by changing the stuck side
z-m-07-06.thinking.2: Tell how the stuck side affects the perimeter
z-m-07-06.prereq.0: Know the meaning of right triangle and rectangle (Grade 3 level)
z-m-07-06.prereq.1: The perimeter of a shape is the length once around its edge
z-m-07-06.s.s1.prompt: What do you think of what Seoa said?
z-m-07-06.s.s1.hint.0: Make two right triangles (3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm) from paper and draw the shapes you get as you change the stuck side. If you have no paper, picture a right angle like a corner of a book and do it in your head.
z-m-07-06.s.s1.hint.1: In the stuck shape, check whether all four angles are right angles and whether it has four sides.
z-m-07-06.s.s1.o.a: It depends on how you stick them
z-m-07-06.s.s1.r.a: This is a judgment that you will check by changing the stuck side and the direction you place it. It gets clearer if you find in which cases it becomes a rectangle.
z-m-07-06.s.s1.o.b: You can't know before sticking them
z-m-07-06.s.s1.r.b: You know the right angles and the side lengths, so you can work it out in your head even before sticking the paper. Recall whether all four angles of a rectangle are right angles.
z-m-07-06.s.s1.o.c: However you stick them, it never becomes a rectangle
z-m-07-06.s.s1.r.c: Did you check whether there is really no way of sticking that makes a rectangle? Look again at the case of sticking the longest sides.
z-m-07-06.s.s1.o.d: However you stick them, it becomes a rectangle
z-m-07-06.s.s1.r.d: This is a judgment that followed Seoa's claim as it is. Also make and check the case of sticking the 3 cm sides yourself.
z-m-07-06.s.s1.explain: If you stick the 5 cm sides, turning one piece, it becomes a rectangle 3 cm wide and 4 cm tall. If you stick the 3 cm sides, flipping one piece gives a big triangle and turning one piece gives a slanted four-sided shape, so it's not a rectangle. So it depends on the stuck side and the way.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.prompt: Let's find the perimeter of the stuck shape. The sum of all three side lengths of one right triangle is 12 cm. When sticking sides of equal length, let the length of the stuck side be j cm (one of 3, 4, 5), and find two different cases where the perimeter of the shape you make is longer than 14 cm.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.hint.0: First find the total of the perimeters of the two pieces.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.hint.1: Check with paper whether the stuck side stays on the edge of the shape, and subtract the length that doesn't stay.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a side that can be stuck.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The stuck side must be one of 3, 4, 5 cm. The two are identical, so you stick sides of the same length.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The perimeter is longer than 14 cm.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The perimeter is not longer than 14 cm. Look at whether there is a side hidden when stuck.
z-m-07-06.s.s2.explain: The perimeter of one piece is 3+4+5=12 cm, so two pieces make 24 cm. The stuck side goes inside and is hidden on both pieces. Sticking the 3 cm side gives 24−6=18 cm, the 4 cm side gives 24−8=16 cm, and the 5 cm side gives 24−10=14 cm. A perimeter longer than 14 cm comes from sticking the 3 cm or 4 cm side.
z-m-07-06.s.s3.prompt: What would you like to tell Seoa? Give one way of sticking that makes a rectangle and one that does not, and write which side you stuck and how.
z-m-07-06.s.s3.hint.0: Recall the cases of sticking the 3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm sides that you used when finding the perimeter, one at a time.
z-m-07-06.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many right angles the shape has after sticking.
z-m-07-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check with the four angles that the shape made by the sticking you described really is (or isn't) a rectangle?
z-m-07-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write clearly which side is stuck, by its length?
z-m-07-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write knowing that one counterexample is enough to break 'always'?
z-m-07-06.s.s3.model.0: It's not always like that. If you stick the 5 cm sides and turn one piece, you get a rectangle 3 cm wide and 4 cm tall, but if you stick the 3 cm sides, it's not a rectangle.
z-m-07-06.s.s3.model.1: It depends on the stuck side. If you stick the longest sides you can make a rectangle, but if you stick the short 4 cm sides it's not a rectangle.
z-m-07-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: Writing just 'short side' is fine, but writing the length makes it clearer.

z-m-07-07.title: When does the '75-minute class' in the swimming notice end?
z-m-07-07.topic: Calculating time of day and time length (minutes) and reading a notice
z-m-07-07.goal: Examine whether the time information in a notice fixes the ending time to one, point out the missing information (whether the break is included), and rewrite the notice so guardians won't misunderstand.
z-m-07-07.material:
The swimming class notice says this.
'Class starts at 3:40 p.m. The class is 75 minutes long, and there is a 10-minute break in the middle of the class.'
The guardians' meeting starts at 5:00 p.m. The class must end at exactly 5:00 p.m. or earlier for guardians to go to the meeting. (3:40 is read 'three forty.')
z-m-07-07.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is enough
z-m-07-07.thinking.1: Find several times that fit the conditions
z-m-07-07.thinking.2: Rewrite an ambiguous sentence thinking of the reader
z-m-07-07.prereq.0: Reading time of day and time length (hours and minutes), and that 1 hour is 60 minutes (Grade 3 level)
z-m-07-07.s.s1.prompt: Can the notice alone fix the time the class ends to one? What more would you need to know to fix it?
z-m-07-07.s.s1.hint.0: First find the time 75 minutes after 3:40.
z-m-07-07.s.s1.hint.1: Split into the case where the 10-minute break is inside the 75 minutes and the case where it is added separately, and compare the ending times.
z-m-07-07.s.s1.o.a: You need to know more about the time the class starts
z-m-07-07.s.s1.r.a: The starting time (3:40 p.m.) is already written in the notice. Look at what hasn't been fixed yet.
z-m-07-07.s.s1.o.b: You need to know whether the break is included in the 75 minutes
z-m-07-07.s.s1.r.b: Depending on whether the break is inside the class time, the ending time differs by 10 minutes. If you split the two cases and compare the ending times, you see the use of this question.
z-m-07-07.s.s1.o.c: You need to know how long it takes from the pool to home
z-m-07-07.s.s1.r.c: The time to get home has nothing to do with the time the class ends. The ending time is set by the class time itself.
z-m-07-07.s.s1.o.d: It can be fixed. All the needed numbers are there
z-m-07-07.s.s1.r.d: Even with all the numbers, the sentence doesn't fix how those numbers should be connected. Think about where the break goes.
z-m-07-07.s.s1.explain: If the break is inside the 75 minutes, it ends at 4:55 p.m., and if not, it ends 10 minutes later at 5:05. The notice doesn't tell which. For the condition of ending at exactly 5:00 or earlier, this difference matters.
z-m-07-07.s.s2.prompt: If we count the class of 75 minutes and the break of 10 minutes separately, the class is 85 minutes in all. For the class to end at exactly 5:00 p.m. or earlier, what minute after 3 o'clock must the class start? Write three different starting times in 5-minute steps. (For 3:s, write s. s is 0 or more and 59 or less.)
z-m-07-07.s.s2.hint.0: Change 85 minutes into hours and minutes.
z-m-07-07.s.s2.hint.1: Pick a starting time, find what time it is 85 minutes later, and compare whether it is before 5:00 sharp.
z-m-07-07.s.s2.var.s: Starting time: 3 o'clock and some minutes p.m.
z-m-07-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Make s a natural number from 0 to 59.
z-m-07-07.s.s2.ok.c3: The class ends at exactly 5:00 p.m. or earlier.
z-m-07-07.s.s2.fail.c3: The class ends after 5 o'clock. Try starting earlier.
z-m-07-07.s.s2.explain: 85 minutes is 1 hour 25 minutes. 1 hour 25 minutes before 5:00 sharp is 3:35. So if the class starts at 3:35 or earlier, it ends at exactly 5:00 or earlier. In 5-minute steps, 3:00, 3:05, ... up to 3:35 all work.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite the notice so there is no misunderstanding. You can decide yourself whether the break is inside the 75 minutes or not. So that guardians who read it can tell the ending time as one, say the class starts at 3:40 p.m., and write clearly the ending time and where the break fits.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.hint.0: Find the time 75 minutes after 3:40, and decide whether to add the 10-minute break on top.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.hint.1: Rewrite in one sentence the part of the first notice that could be read two ways.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The class starts at 3:40 p.m. and ...
z-m-07-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the ending time you wrote in the notice match the explanation you chose (whether the break is included)?
z-m-07-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is the part that people reading the first notice read two ways now readable only one way?
z-m-07-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write both the starting and ending times, clearly stating hours and minutes?
z-m-07-07.s.s3.model.0: The class starts at 3:40 p.m. and ends at 5:05. The 75-minute class and the 10-minute break are counted separately, so it is 85 minutes in all.
z-m-07-07.s.s3.modelNote.0: This is a notice for the case where the break is counted separately.

z-m-07-08.title: Can we know the combined result without knowing each class's number of votes?
z-m-07-08.topic: Reading the results of two votes together (information about the difference)
z-m-07-08.goal: Know that the information needed when combining votes is not 'each class's number of votes' but 'how many more,' and check and explain by making several examples with different numbers of votes.
z-m-07-08.material:
Class 1 and Class 2 of Grade 3 decided their field trip place by voting. The places are the zoo and the museum, and each person cast only one vote.
Class 1 result: The zoo got 3 more votes than the museum.
Class 2 result: The museum got 2 more votes than the zoo.
We don't yet know how many votes came out in total in each class, or how many votes the zoo and the museum each got. The school decided to combine the votes of both classes and go with whichever has more.
z-m-07-08.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is enough
z-m-07-08.thinking.1: Make several examples that satisfy the conditions yourself
z-m-07-08.prereq.0: Reading the number of votes for each item in a table and comparing them (Grade 3 level)
z-m-07-08.prereq.1: The experience of looking at vote results by combining two classes
z-m-07-08.s.s1.prompt: If we combine the votes of the two classes, which place has how many more votes? Can we tell?
z-m-07-08.s.s1.hint.0: Choose one set of votes that fits Class 1's result and one set that fits Class 2's result, and combine the votes of the two classes.
z-m-07-08.s.s1.hint.1: Choose the numbers of votes differently once more and compare whether the combined difference changes.
z-m-07-08.s.s1.o.a: We can't tell. We need to know each class's number of votes
z-m-07-08.s.s1.r.a: Even without knowing each class's number of votes, if you know just 'how many more votes,' you can find the combined difference. Choose one example of vote numbers and combine them yourself.
z-m-07-08.s.s1.o.b: It's a tie. Each won once
z-m-07-08.s.s1.r.b: It's decided not by the number of times each class won but by the combined number of votes. Winning by 3 votes and winning by 2 votes are different sizes.
z-m-07-08.s.s1.r.c: Think about where 3 and 5 come from. In Class 2, the museum had more. How should that difference be reflected in the combined result?
z-m-07-08.s.s1.r.d: This is a judgment that worked out what the combined difference is when the zoo had more in one class and the museum in the other. Choose one example and check.
z-m-07-08.s.s1.explain: For example, if Class 1 is 14 votes to 11 and Class 2 is 9 votes to 11, combined the zoo has 23 votes and the museum 22, so the zoo has 1 more vote. If Class 1 is 5 votes to 2 and Class 2 is 3 votes to 5, the zoo has 8 and the museum 7, again a 1-vote difference. Even if each class's number of votes differs, if you know only 'how many more,' the combined difference is 1 vote, the difference between 3 votes and 2 votes.

Class 1 has z1 votes for the zoo and b1 for the museum, and Class 2 has z2 votes for the zoo and b2 for the museum. Each class has 30 or fewer voters.

z-m-07-08.s.s2.hint.1: Choose Class 2 too, then compare the combined zoo and museum votes of the two classes.

z-m-07-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Make the numbers of votes natural numbers of 0 or more.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.ok.c2: In Class 1, the zoo has 3 more votes.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.fail.c2: In Class 1, the zoo votes must be exactly 3 more than the museum votes.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.ok.c3: In Class 2, the museum has 2 more votes.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.fail.c3: In Class 2, the museum votes must be exactly 2 more than the zoo votes.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.ok.c4: Each class has 30 or fewer voters.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.fail.c4: One class has more than 30 voters. Reduce the numbers of votes.

z-m-07-08.s.s2.fail.c5: The combined difference of the two classes is not 1 vote. Check the earlier conditions again.
z-m-07-08.s.s2.explain: Even if the numbers of votes differ, as in 14·11·9·11, 5·2·3·5, 16·13·10·12, Class 1's difference is 3 votes (zoo), Class 2's difference is 2 votes (museum), and combined the zoo always has 1 more vote. Even if the numbers of votes differ, the combined difference is the same.
z-m-07-08.s.s3.prompt: A friend said, 'We don't know each class's number of votes, so we can't know the combined result.' How would you like to answer? Using the example (numbers) you just made, write separately what we can know and what we still can't know.

z-m-07-08.s.s3.hint.1: Divide what your friend said into the part that is right (we don't know each number of votes) and the part that is wrong.
z-m-07-08.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Even without knowing the number of votes, ...
z-m-07-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In your example, did you calculate again to check that the differences in Class 1 and Class 2 really are 3 votes and 2 votes?
z-m-07-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you tell apart not knowing the number of votes and knowing the difference?
z-m-07-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also write separately what can't be known from combining (for example, how many votes the zoo got)?
z-m-07-08.s.s3.model.0: We can know it even without knowing the number of votes. Class 1 has 14 and 11 votes, so the zoo has 3 more, and Class 2 has 9 and 11 votes, so the museum has 2 more. Combined, the zoo has 23 votes and the museum 22, so the zoo has 1 more vote.
z-m-07-08.s.s3.modelNote.0: This answer didn't separately say that each place's number of votes differs from example to example.
z-m-07-08.s.s3.model.1: No. All you need to know is how many more. Combining 3 more and 2 more, the zoo has 1 more vote. It's the same even if the number of voters in each class differs.
z-m-07-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: It would be even better to say separately that we can't know how many votes the zoo got.

z-m-07-09.title: How many red bean buns should the bakery bake next Monday?
z-m-07-09.topic: Guessing what's ahead from sales records (handling an outlier)
z-m-07-09.goal: Know that when guessing what's ahead from records, how to handle an outlier depends on the reason, and revise your guess and how much you trust it with new information, writing it in a note.
z-m-07-09.material: A neighborhood bakery bakes the red bean buns to sell that day every morning. If it bakes too many, some are left over, and if it bakes too few, it runs short. The owner wants to decide how many red bean buns to bake next Monday by looking at last week's sales records. Last week the shop was open every day from Monday to Friday.
z-m-07-09.thinking.0: Guess the typical size from data
z-m-07-09.thinking.1: Handle an outlier by examining its reason
z-m-07-09.thinking.2: Keep or revise your judgment with new information
z-m-07-09.thinking.3: Tell situations where your guess could change
z-m-07-09.prereq.0: Reading numbers from tables or records and telling numbers that are close together from outliers (Grade 3 level)
z-m-07-09.s.s1.prompt: Let's guess how many to bake next Monday as we learn the sales records little by little. At each step, choose what you think is most fitting.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write the sales numbers of the days known so far in order, and mark numbers that are close to each other and numbers that stand apart.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.hint.1: If there is a number that stands apart, think of a way to check whether something else happened on that day.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.0.info: They sold 12 on Monday, 14 on Tuesday, and 13 on Wednesday.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: About how many red bean buns would be good to bake next Monday?
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.0.after: The three days are similar at 12 to 14, so about 13, or a bit more generously about 14, is reasonable. Since we've seen only 3 days, 'I want to watch a bit longer' can be considered, but even the current records let us state a rough size.
z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: The sales of the three days are close, 12 to 14, so this judgment picked around the middle.

z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is a careful attitude. Still, looking at how close the numbers of the three days are to each other can give a clue.

z-m-07-09.s.s1.st.1.r.c: An outlier is also a record, so it is counted, but the value pulls the average up. We don't know yet whether next Monday will be a day like Thursday.

z-m-07-10.title: If Seoha's and Haram's results are different, are the two bags different too?
z-m-07-10.topic: Results can differ even under the same conditions (possibility)
z-m-07-10.goal: Know that you can't conclude two bags are different from a few results of 10 draws, and tell how far results work as clues and how to check further.
z-m-07-10.material:
There are two bags with red marbles and blue marbles mixed in them (Bag 가, Bag 나). We don't know how many marbles are in each bag or whether the two bags are the same or different. Seoha took one marble from Bag 가 and Haram took one from Bag 나, looked at its color, and put it back, doing this 10 times each.
Bag 가 (Seoha): red 7 times, blue 3 times
Bag 나 (Haram): red 4 times, blue 6 times
Seoha said, 'My bag has more red and Haram's bag has more blue. The two bags are different!'
z-m-07-10.thinking.0: Examine whether results alone allow a conclusion
z-m-07-10.thinking.1: Evaluate ways of finding out more
z-m-07-10.thinking.2: Organize and write your judgment and its evidence
z-m-07-10.prereq.0: Count what can happen by number of times and organize it in a table
z-m-07-10.s.s1.prompt: What do you think of what Seoha said? Choose the most fitting one based on this result alone.
z-m-07-10.s.s1.hint.0: Write Seoha's result and Haram's result side by side in a table.
z-m-07-10.s.s1.hint.1: Suppose the two drew from the same bag, and think about whether such results could come out.
z-m-07-10.s.s1.o.a: Bag 가 has more red, and Bag 나 has more blue
z-m-07-10.s.s1.r.a: This is a judgment that accepted Seoha's statement as it is. Think about whether results of 10 draws could differ this much even from the same bag.
z-m-07-10.s.s1.o.b: Nothing can be said from the drawn results
z-m-07-10.s.s1.r.b: A result is also a clue. You can say that the side where red came up more has a slightly higher chance of having more red. Concluding and ignoring the clue are different.
z-m-07-10.s.s1.o.c: From just 10 draws, you can't conclude the two bags are different
z-m-07-10.s.s1.r.c: This is a judgment that accepts the results as a clue but sees a need to check more. Recall whether results can differ even from the same bag.
z-m-07-10.s.s1.o.d: There are 7 red marbles and 6 blue marbles
z-m-07-10.s.s1.r.d: The number of times drawn is not the number of marbles. The marble was put back after taking it out, so the same marble may have been drawn many times.
z-m-07-10.s.s1.explain: Even from the same bag, if you draw 10 times each, red may come up 7 times or 4 times. So even if the results differ, you can't conclude the two bags are different. But that doesn't mean the results are no clue at all. You can say that the side where red came up more has a slightly higher chance of having more red.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.prompt: What methods would help to find out better whether the two bags are the same or different? Choose all the helpful methods.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.hint.0: For each method, write what new information you would learn after using it.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.hint.1: Compare how trusting the first results differs from collecting new results.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.o.a: Each increases the number of draws and combines the results
z-m-07-10.s.s2.r.a: As the number of draws grows, the results tend to get closer to the ratio of marbles in the bag, so the clue becomes more trustworthy.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.o.b: Trust the side where red came up more in the current results
z-m-07-10.s.s2.r.b: Trusting existing results as they are adds no new information, so it doesn't make the first judgment any surer.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.o.c: Each of the two draws just one more time
z-m-07-10.s.s2.r.c: One more draw result can tell almost nothing. You need results from many draws to have a clue.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.o.d: Take out all the marbles and count them by color
z-m-07-10.s.s2.r.d: If you take them out and count directly, you can be most sure whether the two bags are the same. But if it is a game where you can't take them out, you can't use it.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.explain: Increasing the number of draws and combining makes the clue trustworthy, and taking out and counting all the marbles confirms it directly. Trusting the current results as they are or drawing just one more time tells almost no new information.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.acc.0: If it is a game where you can't take them out and count, increasing the number of draws and combining is the best method.
z-m-07-10.s.s2.acc.1: If you take them out and count, you can know for sure. It would also be good to think of the method of increasing the number of draws, in case you can't take them out.
z-m-07-10.s.s3.prompt: What would you like to tell Seoha? Write what to do to check further, while respecting Seoha's result.
z-m-07-10.s.s3.hint.0: Start from the fact that Seoha and Haram each drew 10 times.
z-m-07-10.s.s3.hint.1: Divide Seoha's result into the part you can trust and the part you can't be sure of yet.
z-m-07-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you value Seoha's result (7 times) without concluding?
z-m-07-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is there something you compared with Haram's result?
z-m-07-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Does the way of checking you described really add new information?
z-m-07-10.s.s3.model.0: Seoha, 7 out of 10 might mean there is more red. But Haram got 4, so even from the same bag a difference this size can happen. Let's both increase the number of draws and combine them.
z-m-07-10.s.s3.model.1: We can't conclude they are different yet. We only tried 10 draws each, so if we draw more and compare how many times red came up, we can tell better.
z-m-07-10.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is a case that didn't mention Seoha's result directly but didn't conclude and described a method.
